source: David Faris, The Glasgow Family of Adams County, Ohio (Baltimore: Gateway Press, 1990), printed pp.8–15; FamilySearch catalogue koha:646654, film 2055438 Item 5, DGS 007834162, images 1564–1567, visually inspected 23 October 2026. This is an inspected published genealogy, not inspection of its cited original letters or wills. The film’s generic Tennessee metadata does not describe this book item. The letters are cross-referenced on p.13 to pp.20–21; those pages were not inspected in this batch, so the maintained letter transcription remains the source for its wording.
basis: The actual Faris book has now been inspected, rather than only its catalogue abstract. Printed p.11 uses a dotted possible connection from James of Moneymore to the American brothers; p.12 explicitly reports that evidence for Robert and his brothers’ parentage had not been found. James was the author’s identifiable County Londonderry candidate, not an evidenced father. The retrospective Irish pedigree on pp.8–9 and Samuel’s 1824 Pennsylvania will discussed on p.12 identify an Irish sibling group, including William, James and Robert remaining in Ireland, without joining it to the emigrant brothers. County setting, a compatible generation and the existing family tradition keep James a plausible candidate, but cannot sustain the earlier probable father assessment.
limitations: Robert, Arthur and Joseph’s established brotherhood remains separately supported by the maintained 1806 letter transcription and Joseph’s 1831 will. John of Peters Township remains a probable brother at 83%; Faris p.15 also reconstructs the four brothers from the 1779–1780 tax/probate cluster. These sibling arguments do not identify their father. The 1824 Samuel will has been read only through Faris’s excerpt, not its manuscript. The Irish Robert in that will/pedigree is not identified as the emigrant Robert born in 1749. All mothers, upstream ancestry, life dates and current attachments are preserved; no live WikiTree save or identity merge follows. Exact percentages are subjective pair-specific judgments, not measured frequencies or multiplied probabilities.
scope: Existing father-profile propositions only: Robert-12 85% → 35%; Arthur-649 and Joseph-1543 each 82% → 35%; John-4027 76% → 30%; Mary-4030 64% → 22%. All five were probable; the first four are now possible and Mary uncertain. James-1024 remains the selected named candidate; no attachment is removed. James-1024’s own older father stays 18%, and Samuel-1492’s father stays 23%.

prior.source_basis: The existing Moneymore father account, Glasgow-1024, is assessed as the probable father of Robert Glasgow-12 and, by inference through their established brotherhood, Arthur Glasgow-649 and Joseph Glasgow-1543. The catalogue description of David Faris’s 1990 genealogy explicitly identifies the Adams County emigrant Robert (1749–1839) as a son of a James resident at Moneymore. It identifies a particular father and son, rather than offering a same-name local candidate. The family letter of 6 November 1806 printed by Faris names Arthur and Robert as Joseph’s brothers; Joseph’s 1831 will independently identifies Arthur as his deceased brother and the younger Robert as Arthur’s son. These sources distinguish the two Roberts and establish the sibling group to which the father attribution can reasonably extend. Robert’s pension supports the County Derry setting and 1769 migration. The approximate generations are compatible; the circa-1722 birth estimate is not independent evidence. The positive father attribution and established family group together warrant probable parentage, while remaining below documented or certain.

prior.source_basis: Assess James of Moneymore, Glasgow-1024, as John of Peters Township’s probable father at 76%. The 2024 Adams County family account specifically identifies the John who died in 1779 as brother of Robert, Arthur and Joseph. Fendrick’s abstract independently supplies a contemporary Joseph Glasgow witness in John’s Peters Township will; James Neely’s presence also fits the later Neely-associated emigrant family. Faris’s catalogue description identifies Robert’s father as James of Moneymore and reports four emigrant brothers. Together these identify a specific compatible family, rather than only another local James. Extend that probable father across the preferred fourth-brother identification, while rating John lower than the three established brothers because his place in that group depends partly on the later account and witness identification. Assess the John-to-each-established-brother relationship as probable at 83%.

cross_source_review.note: PRONI D2003 introduction identifies John as a Bannside weaver and Jean McClure as from Drumack in the Braid. The held diary, 14 August1858, p.29, names Crawford landlords and Mr Doads of Clough in a voluntary-payment matter; neither an exact holding nor John’s father is named. The collection introduction describes Glasgow-family volumes and later copies but does not identify a surviving receipt or specific file for that payment. John’s father remains unknown; James’s father John remains96%.
